This extended dependency is consistent with patterns observed in other ctenomyids, where the demands of digging and the challenges of the subterranean environment shape the developmental schedule.

The ultimate wet weight of an adult Magellanic tuco-tuco averages 184.2 grams [Wwi = 184.2 grams], placing it among the medium-sized members of its genus. This body mass is achieved after a prolonged growth period, reflecting a life-history strategy oriented toward delayed reproduction and extended somatic investment. The reproductive frequency is low, with females producing on average approximately 4 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 4 litters per year], resulting in a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 12 to 20 offspring.

The lifespan of the Magellanic tuco-tuco is comparatively extended for a rodent of its body size, with maximum longevity recorded at 730 days [am = 730 days] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The interplay between this high metabolic demand, the extended gestation period, and the low reproductive rate defines the species' position along the slow-fast continuum of life-history strategies.
